Israeli forces close a military checkpoint near the Palestinian town of Taybeh, east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, on 23 August 2026, after shooting and wounding a Palestinian man from the nearby village of Burqa (Zain Jaafar/AFP)
Off
Every afternoon at exactly 4pm, a calculated military decision transforms the exits of Ramallah and al-Bireh into an open-air gridlock of vehicles piled nose to tail, idling engines and mounting frustration.
What Israeli authorities continue to market to the world as temporary "security measures" - the iron gates, concrete barriers, earth mounds and armed checkpoints choking the occupied West Bank - has long since metastasised into a deliberate, institutionalised apparatus of spatial segregation and racial discrimination.
This architecture of control does not exist to neutralise genuine threats. It operates to clear shared arterial roads for Israeli settlers at the exact hour Palestinian civilian movement reaches its daily peak.
By subordinating the basic right of an indigenous population to travel through its own land, the system grants permanent priority to one group while punishing another for the simple act of trying to commute home after a day's work.
According to comprehensive field documentation compiled by the United Nations' humanitarian office, Ocha, and the human rights organisation B'Tselem, the landscape of the occupied West Bank is carved up by more than 900 fixed and intermittent movement obstacles.
They comprise permanently manned military checkpoints, partial ones, remote-controlled iron gates, earth mounds, roadblocks and trenches, which restrict and dictate the daily lives of 3.4 million Palestinians.

US taxpayer group calls on ICC to investigate Trump, Rubio for 'aiding' Gaza genocide
A group of US taxpayers and international human rights lawyers have officially called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate President Donald Trump and his top diplomat Marco Rubio for "aiding and abetting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed by Israel in Gaza".
They announced it at a press conference at the court's home in The Hague, in the Netherlands, on Wednesday.
The submission to the court was organised by the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), and includes sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, firsthand eyewitness accounts, whistleblower testimony, video evidence, and extensive documentation of what they say is US military, financial, diplomatic, and political support for Israel, the group said.
Among those involved are Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon who undertook two missions in Gaza, and David McIntosh, a former contractor with the scandal-plagued and now-defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, both of whom have previously shared their detailed experiences with Middle East Eye.
It took nearly a year to compile the necessary proof that without the US, Israel could not have carried out what the United Nations and Holocaust scholars have described as a genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, Taag said in a press release accompanying the announcement.

Saudi Arabia faces liquidity crunch even as oil exports rebound to pre-war levels
Saudi Arabia is feeling the pinch of a liquidity crisis as bank deposits slow and the economy comes under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, a new report from Bank of America says.
In a note to clients, Bank of America said Saudi Arabia is grappling with “contagion” caused by liquidity tightness in the UAE and a rapid slowdown in the kingdom’s own economy, according to an article published on Bloomberg on Tuesday.
The report said Saudi banks are feeling the pain in the UAE, which is also grappling with fallout from the Iran war and tighter liquidity. Saudi banks are closely linked to their Emirati neighbours, with a high number of interbank transactions contributing to deposits at Saudi banks.
At the same time, the Saudi economy is under strain and government entities are making withdrawals from Saudi banks. But loan demand is high, which is effectively raising the cost of Saudi money.
The liquidity strain is notable for Saudi Arabia because its currency is directly pegged to the US dollar, along with Gulf states including the UAE, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain.

Revealed: West Bank petrol station chain faces $325m claim in PA fuel-smuggling probe
A petrol station chain owned by one of the West Bank’s wealthiest businessmen is facing accusations of alleged fuel smuggling, financial misconduct and tax evasion totalling more than 1bn shekels ($325m), according to a leaked report seen by Middle East Eye.
The investigation, which has unfolded against a backdrop of worsening fuel shortages in the occupied Palestinian territory, has led to the arrest and weeks-long detention of Tarek al-Natsheh, the chairman of Al-Huda Group, as well as raids by security forces on his company’s offices and the confiscation of computers and financial records.
Lawyers for Natsheh, who is accused in the report of profiting from smuggling activities, say he denies wrongdoing and stands ready to pay any taxes he may legally owe.
They say the company and Natsheh are cooperating with legal proceedings, but have criticised his detention, commenting that “personal freedom should not be used as a means of pressure to accept figures whose accuracy has not been established”.
MEE sent a detailed list of questions and a request for comment to Malek al-Awri, legal adviser for the defence team, ahead of publication of this article. Awri referred MEE to a previous statement he had given to the Palestinian Watan newspaper last month.

El-Quseir is filled with crumbling Ottoman-era houses with protruding wooden balconies (MEE/Sean Mathews)
Off
El-Quseir is pitch black at night. The only light inside this decaying labyrinth of a port comes when a battered Bajaj motorcycle purrs down the odd alley, casting a headlight on one of the town’s many stray dogs, or a passerby flashes a phone, lighting up a decaying wooden balcony.
The old mayor’s house is easy to find in the darkness. It emits a warm, golden light. When I arrive, a crowd is already gathered on the colonnaded veranda; some men in djellabas, others in the uniform skinny jeans of the Middle East.
I spot the odd Cairo hipster among them. The women attendees are especially radiant in make-up. Why shouldn’t they be.
Tonight is a Hazz night, the name, which in Arabic means luck, given to soirees down Egypt’s Red Sea coast, where the simsimiyya , a triangular lyre, is played to ballads about old ports, friendships and legendary seafarers.
The simsimiyya looms large over El-Quseir.
“The men here would be at sea for four months at a time. They would save a spot on their dhow just for a simsimiyya player to entertain them,” Aly El-Sayed, the founder of Bahar, a community organisation working to preserve the city's heritage and marine ecosystem, told me.
Aly is the host of tonight’s gathering. The old mayor’s house, a butter-yellow bungalow built in 1888, has been repurposed as Bahar’s home.
“We tried not to change much. We were even careful not to paint too much,” El-Sayed said.
'They sang all the time'
I knew that music was central to life aboard dhows, traditional wooden sailing boats, that plied goods, including slaves, between East Africa and Arabia up until the mid-20th century.

“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” UN secretary general Antonio Guterres told world leaders at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Wednesday.
The UN chief siad that the slow international response to the climate crisis had put the world on this path and that rapid action was needed to avert it.
His comments set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders at the UN conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, Reuters reported.
Guterres pointed to rising carbon emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters in his speech.
“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs.”
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.
The summit opened on Monday and has, relative to its importance, received little attention against a backdrop of numerous wars, rampant inflation and other crises.
Rapidly rising global temperatures feed into these other crises, driving conflict and competition for resources. Oil and gas companies have profited hugely from the war on Iran, which has driven up the price of fossil fuels.

Analysis: The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
ne of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
The trauma of the Hamas-led 7 October attack may have bypassed the Haredi spiritual leadership and its veteran MPs, but the wider Haredi public, including the generally more conservative Lithuanian community, understands that something momentous has happened in Israel. This is particularly true of the younger generation.

One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
This social model developed in Israel, where Torah study in yeshivas and kollelim has become a central way of life and even a social ideal for Haredi men. Many devote years to religious study instead of entering the labour market or undertaking military service.
The model rests on the belief that Torah study is a supreme value and a communal obligation, supported financially by families, the community, the state and religious support networks.
For decades, the Haredi parties were among the most stable and predictable blocs in Israeli politics. One of the world’s leading scholars of Ottoman history, Engin Deniz Akarli, died in his home in Istanbul on Sunday, aged 81.
Professor Akarli’s research focused on the legal, political and economic history of the late Ottoman Empire, as well as the Middle East. His scholarship engaged deeply with neglected areas of research in these fields.
One of his most influential works, The Long Peace: Ottoman Lebanon, 1861-1920 (University of California Press, 1993) challenged Eurocentric narratives on state-building and governance that centre western intervention through a close study of the Mount Lebanon Mutassarifiya (governorate) following the civil war of 1860.
He demonstrated that Lebanese self-rule, institutions and local religious reconciliation in this period laid the foundations for secular democracy that was hampered by European intervention.
Born in the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, Professor Akarli completed his primary and secondary education at Eskisehir Maarif College, and graduated from the Department of Business Administration and Economics at the prestigious Robert College (now Bogazici University), in 1968.
He continued his education in the United States, first at Wisconsin University for his Master’s studies, and then at Princeton for his PhD.
His teaching career spanned several universities multiple continents. After completing his doctoral studies, he returned to Turkey as one of the founding professors of the history department at Bogazici University.

Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
Iran defended a proposal on Monday to restart peace talks in as few as two days as the most reasonable offer on the table, after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called some of Iran's conditions "outrageous and ridiculous".
"Is it unreasonable that Iran demands that US illegal sanctions and its naval blockade must be lifted before negotiations start and that the war should end on all fronts?" Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference in response to Rubio's remarks.
Iran has made the offer to shorten the time to restart talks from an earlier seven-day proposal, which calls for Washington to first meet conditions including halting hostilities, lifting a blockade and waiving sanctions.
Baghaei also said US pressure on Iraq to close most of its borders with Iran should not affect bilateral ties with Baghdad, after Iraq's foreign minister said Washington was pushing for such a move. Baghaei dismissed a US military task force aimed at restricting Iran's land trade as a diversion following President Donald Trump's Republicans' losses in midterm elections.
Reporting by Reuters

A sand embankment collapsed on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip late on Sunday, killing three children and two women as severe weather battered the territory.
At least five other people were rescued with injuries by Civil Defence search-and-rescue teams at the makeshift camp in Deir al-Balah, where operations to locate missing people continued.
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence in Gaza, said the massive sandy embankment and surrounding mounds of earth collapsed after a low-pressure weather system brought torrential rain and strong winds to the Strip over the weekend.
Two of those killed were identified as Mariam Nabhan and her son, Salah Nabhan. The other three were Reem al-Zain, Habiba al-Zain and Ibrahim al-Zain.
Weekend downpours flooded an estimated 70,000 temporary tents sheltering displaced families across Gaza, leaving thousands of people exposed to the elements.
Palestinians have blamed Israel’s genocide and ongoing siege for the worsening conditions facing displaced people.
“This is not simply the result of severe weather. It is the direct consequence of prolonged Israeli genocide, the widespread destruction of infrastructure, continued displacement, and the denial of essential humanitarian assistance and adequate shelter,” the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Saturday.
The ministry said nearly two million Palestinians were living in approximately 270,000 tents across Gaza in “appalling humanitarian conditions”.
